title: Inside a search cluster: OpenSearch nodes, shards and replicas
goal: By the end you can explain how OpenSearch splits an index into a fixed number of primary shards and replicas and routes each document by a hash of its id, why every search is a scatter-gather over local indexes, what the elected cluster manager does, how a write reaches every copy and a search fans out and merges, what a node failure does to cluster health, and how to size shards and set up a three-node cluster.

warmup.q: An index has 3 primary shards and 1 replica, on three nodes. One node is switched off. What does a search for every merchant return a few seconds later?
options: About two thirds of the merchants: the stopped node's shards are gone
Every merchant, because each shard still has a copy on a running node
An error until the node comes back
Every merchant, but only after the cluster has copied the missing shards
warmup.why: The stopped node held one copy each of two shards, and each of those shards has its other copy on a running node. The cluster manager promotes a replica wherever a primary went missing, so every shard has a primary and every document is searchable: health is yellow. Copying new replicas comes later, after a one-minute wait, and only restores redundancy. Losing data needs both copies of a shard to go.

sections.h: One node runs out, so split the index into shards and copy each one
sections.body:
The track's last case study is a search cluster, and it puts lesson 4 at the centre. A search index is a local secondary index taken to its limit: every shard holds an inverted index of its own documents only, so every search is a scatter-gather over all of them. Around that sit ideas from earlier lessons: hash routing over a fixed number of shards (lessons 1 and 3), copies of each shard behind a single leader (the Replication track's first lesson), and an elected node that holds the map of who owns what (lesson 3).

The OpenSearch in the Storage engines track's lesson on indexes for text, time and vectors was one node holding one index in one shard: `number_of_shards: 1, number_of_replicas: 0`. For five merchants that's right. Now put the dispute notes behind it, 30 million documents and about 120 GB of index that grows every month, and three things go wrong. One machine's disk and memory become a ceiling the index keeps pushing against. Every search runs on the one node, so its CPUs cap the searches per second. And when the node reboots for a kernel patch, search is down until it's back.

Version 1 is a bigger machine. It buys time for the first two problems, does nothing for the third, and gets expensive fast.

Version 2 splits the index. OpenSearch divides an index into a fixed number of primary shards, and each shard is a complete Lucene index: its own inverted index of posting lists, the structure from that lesson. The shards spread over the nodes, so three nodes hold a third each and search in parallel. Each document lives in exactly one shard, chosen by a hash of its routing value, which is its `_id` unless you say otherwise:

```text
shard = hash(_routing) % number_of_primary_shards
```

That modulo is why the primary count is fixed when you create the index. Change 3 to 4 and almost every document hashes to a different shard: lesson 2 measured `hash mod S` moving 80% of the keys. That is lesson 3's fixed-shard-count design, with the count fixed per index, and OpenSearch won't move documents for you. You create a new index and reindex into it, or `_split` the index into a multiple of its shard count, 3 into 6. The split works because the formula above is a shorthand. OpenSearch actually hashes into 768 routing slots for a 3-shard index and gives each shard 256 consecutive slots, so splitting 3 into 6 cuts each shard's range in two, and every document lands in one of its old shard's two halves. The lab checks this against the real cluster.

Version 3 copies each shard. A replica is a full copy of a primary on another node, kept up to date on every write. If a node dies, the replica still has the data, and it serves searches too, so more replicas mean more search throughput. The one placement rule is that a replica never sits on the same node as its primary or another copy of its shard, because a copy next to the original protects nothing. Unlike primaries, you can change `number_of_replicas` at any time. An index created with no settings gets 1 primary and 1 replica.

**A search cluster is a map. Each index is a fixed number of primary shards, each a whole Lucene index with replicas on other nodes; one elected cluster manager keeps the map of which copy lives where, and every node uses it to send a write to a primary and a search to one copy of every shard.** The rest of the lesson fills in that picture.

try.title: Start three nodes and see where twelve merchants land
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the cluster: `docker compose -f env/opensearch-cluster.yml up -d --wait`. It takes one to two minutes and about 3 GB of Docker memory. os1 answers on port 9200, os2 on 9201 and os3 on 9202.
Load twelve merchants into an index with 3 primaries and 1 replica: `sh env/opensearch-cluster/nosql-18-merchants.sh`. It prints `{"status":"green"}` once every copy exists.

Run the commands below. Before the third, predict how many of the twelve land in each shard, and whether any node holds both copies of a shard. Leave the cluster running for this lesson's other Try-its.

The twelve merchants split 6, 2 and 4, which is what a hash does with a handful of keys; with millions of documents the shards come out within a fraction of a percent of each other. M-0042 is in shard 2, as the figure works out from its hash. The shard numbers per merchant are the same on every machine, because they depend only on the ids. sections.h: One elected cluster manager keeps the map
sections.body:
Every node in the lab cluster answers `_cat/shards` with the same table, but only one node may change it. That table is part of the cluster state: the list of nodes, every index's settings and mappings, and the routing table that says which copy of which shard lives on which node. Each node keeps a copy of the cluster state and routes requests with it. One node, the elected cluster manager, is the only one that changes it. That is OpenSearch's answer to lesson 3's question of who holds the map. It decides where new shards go, notices when a node disappears, and publishes every new version of the state to all the nodes.

A node's roles say what it may do, and you set them with `node.roles`:

| Role | What the node does |
|---|---|
| `cluster_manager` | may be elected cluster manager (it's "eligible") and votes in elections |
| `data` | holds shards: indexes documents and runs searches on them |
| `ingest` | runs ingest pipelines that reshape documents before they're indexed |
| coordinating | every node: takes a client request, sends it to the right shards, merges the answers |

A node with `node.roles: []` does only the last job. The lab's three nodes are all `cluster_manager` and `data`. In production you'd usually run three small dedicated cluster managers and separate data nodes, so a data node stuck in garbage collection can't stall the cluster state.

How do the eligible nodes agree on one manager? By voting. A candidate becomes manager when a majority of the voting nodes vote for it, and every election starts a new term, the same idea as the terms in Raft, which the Consensus track builds. The manager checks every node once a second and removes one that misses three checks in a row; the other nodes check the manager the same way and start an election when it goes quiet.

Majority is why you need three eligible nodes. With two, a majority is two, so if either fails the other can't win an election, and nothing that needs the manager can happen: no new indices, no replica promotion, no shard allocation. With three, any two carry on. Majority also stops split brain: a network split can leave at most one side with a majority, so two managers never accept conflicting changes.

Two settings bootstrap all this. `discovery.seed_hosts` lists the addresses where a starting node looks for the others. `cluster.initial_cluster_manager_nodes` names the eligible nodes that may vote in the very first election, and it's read only once, when the cluster forms for the first time.

try.title: Stop the cluster manager and watch a new one win
steps: Read the cluster state's version, the current manager's node id and the election term. Then stop whichever node is the manager.
Ask all three ports who the manager is now (the stopped one stays silent), and read the term again. Predict the term before you look.
Bring the node back with `docker compose -f env/opensearch-cluster.yml up -d --wait`; the last command waits until every copy is assigned and nothing is moving.

sections.h: A write goes to the primary, a search to one copy of every shard
sections.body:
Write a new merchant, `PUT merchants/_doc/M-0054`, to any node and that node acts as the coordinator. It hashes `M-0054` (shard 2), looks up shard 2's primary in its cluster state, and forwards the request there. The primary indexes the document into an in-memory buffer and appends the operation to its translog, a write-ahead log on disk that is fsync'ed before the request is acknowledged (`index.translog.durability: request`). Then it sends the operation to every in-sync replica of the shard, in parallel, and waits for all of them to do the same. Only then does the client get its answer, which says `"_shards": {"total": 2, "successful": 2}`: both copies have it. The primary numbers every operation with a sequence number, and a primary term that goes up each time a replica is promoted, so replicas can tell old operations from new ones.

Acknowledged doesn't mean searchable yet. The buffer isn't part of the inverted index. Every second (`index.refresh_interval: 1s`) each shard copy turns its buffer into a new Lucene segment, a small, immutable inverted index of its own, and opens it for searching. That refresh is why OpenSearch is called near-real-time: a document appears in searches up to a second after the write returns. A `GET` by id doesn't wait: it's real-time, and finds the latest version before any refresh. Segments never change once written, so deletes are marks and updates are new versions, and background merges combine small segments into bigger ones, like the compaction in the Storage engines track's LSM tree lesson. A flush is a Lucene commit: it fsyncs the segments and trims the translog.

A search fans out, and lesson 4 says why. A shard's inverted index covers only that shard's documents, so no shard can say which other shards hold matches, and the coordinator has to ask them all. It sends the query to one copy of every shard, primary or replica, picking the copy that has answered fastest lately (adaptive replica selection). That's the query phase: each shard scores its own documents with BM25 and returns only the ids and scores of its best `from + size`. The coordinator merges those lists into the global top, then runs the fetch phase: it asks for the full documents of the page it will return, and nothing else. So `from: 9990, size: 10` on 5 shards makes every shard find its top 10,000 and the coordinator sort 50,000 hits to return 10. That's why `index.max_result_window` stops `from + size` at 10,000 by default; page deeper with `search_after`. And the search is as slow as its slowest shard: if each of 10 shards answers within its own p99 99% of the time, all 10 do so only 0.99^10, about 90%, of the time.

One more effect of fanning out: each shard computes BM25's idf from its own documents only. With millions of documents per shard the statistics agree and nobody notices. With a few documents they don't, and the ranking can change, which the Try-it shows. `search_type=dfs_query_then_fetch` adds a first round trip that collects global statistics.

sections.h: When a node leaves: promote, wait, copy, green
sections.body:
Cluster health is one word for the whole routing table. Green: every primary and every replica is assigned to a node. Yellow: every primary is assigned, but at least one replica isn't, so all the data is there and searchable, with less redundancy than you asked for. Red: at least one primary is unassigned, so some documents can't be searched and writes to that shard fail.

Watch what a node failure does to the map, because every step is a decision the cluster manager makes. The manager notices first: the node misses three follower checks a second apart and is removed from the cluster state. For each primary the node held, the manager promotes an in-sync replica on another node. That's instant, because the replica already has every acknowledged write, and the shard's primary term goes up by one. Every copy the node held is now missing, so the replicas it held and the old primaries' places become unassigned replicas, and health turns yellow.

Then the manager waits. Copying a shard means reading every segment from the primary and writing it to a new node, and if the node was only restarting for a patch, that work is wasted. So for one minute (`index.unassigned.node_left.delayed_timeout`) the unassigned replicas stay unassigned, in case the node comes back with its copies intact. After the minute, the manager allocates each missing replica to a node that holds no copy of that shard, preferring nodes with fewer shards, and the new copy pulls the primary's segments. That's a peer recovery, limited to 40 MB a second per node by default (`indices.recovery.max_bytes_per_sec`), so a 30 GB shard takes about 13 minutes. When every copy is started again, health is green, now on fewer nodes. When the node returns, or a new one joins, the balancer moves copies onto it until the shard counts are even.

Red needs every copy of a shard to go at once: with one replica, two nodes that held a shard's two copies failing before a new copy is built. A brand-new empty node can't fix it. Only the lost node coming back with its disk, or a restore from a snapshot, brings that shard back. Two replicas make it a three-node failure, at the price of a third copy of every byte.

sections.h: Size the shards, then set up the nodes
sections.body:
Now size it. OpenSearch's documentation says to keep shards between 10 and 50 GB, and both limits have reasons. A 200 GB shard is slow to move: at 40 MB a second its peer recovery takes well over an hour, during which the shard has one copy fewer, and one shard's search can't spread over more nodes. Thousands of 100 MB shards fail differently: every shard is a Lucene index with its own files, memory and entry in the cluster state, and every search pays a request per shard. `cluster.max_shards_per_node` stops you at 1,000 shard copies per node by default. So pick the primary count from the size you expect: 120 GB of disputes at about 30 GB a shard is 4 primaries. For data that grows forever, such as logs or authorization events, create one index per day or week and roll over to a new one, so shard sizes stay put and old data leaves by deleting whole indices.

Each node's settings live in `config/opensearch.yml`. The essentials for a three-node cluster:

```yaml
cluster.name: sfz-search            # nodes join only a cluster with the same name
node.name: os1
node.roles: [cluster_manager, data]
network.host: 0.0.0.0               # bind to a real interface, not just localhost
discovery.seed_hosts: [os1, os2, os3]
cluster.initial_cluster_manager_nodes: [os1, os2, os3]   # first start only
path.data: /var/lib/opensearch
```

The heap goes in `config/jvm.options` or `OPENSEARCH_JAVA_OPTS`: `-Xms` equal to `-Xmx`, half the machine's RAM, and no more than about 31 GB, so the JVM keeps compressed object pointers. The other half isn't wasted. Lucene reads most of its segment files through memory-mapped files (from the Operating systems track's lesson on copy-on-write and mmap), so the kernel's page cache holds the hot segments, and a search served from it never touches the disk. Lucene maps many files, which is why Linux needs `vm.max_map_count` of at least 262,144. Once a node binds to a non-loopback address, it enforces that and other bootstrap checks and refuses to start if they fail. Turn swap off. And watch the disk: at 85% full a node gets no new shards, at 90% the manager moves shards away, and at 95% indices on that node become read-only.

The lab switches off the security plugin to keep `curl` simple, so it runs plain HTTP, no TLS between nodes, and no users. Never do that outside a laptop: a real cluster needs TLS on both the HTTP and the node-to-node transport layer, and users and roles.

Elasticsearch works the same way, and the lab runs OpenSearch 3.9.0. OpenSearch began in 2021 as a fork of Elasticsearch 7.10.2, so shards, replicas, routing, refresh and the cluster manager (Elasticsearch still says "master") carry over. The difference is the licence, as the Storage engines track's search lesson said: OpenSearch is Apache 2.0, while Elasticsearch ships under the Elastic License 2.0 with an AGPLv3 option added in 2024.

analogy: A search cluster is a library spread over three branches. Every book series (an index) is split into a fixed number of volumes (primary shards) by the first letter of the title, and each branch holds some volumes plus photocopies (replicas) of volumes kept elsewhere, never a photocopy in the same branch as its original. The head librarian (the cluster manager) keeps the catalogue that says which branch has what, and any branch can take your question, send it to one copy of every volume, and merge the answers. When a branch floods, the photocopies become the originals and the head librarian orders new photocopies. The analogy breaks on the letters: a library can re-split its shelves whenever it likes, but OpenSearch's split comes from a hash fixed at creation, so changing the number of volumes means copying the whole series.
in_your_world: If your payments platform has a search cluster for merchants or disputes, you can read its whole layout with three calls: `_cat/nodes`, `_cat/shards` and `_cluster/health`. Check that three nodes are manager-eligible, that shard sizes sit between 10 and 50 GB, and that nothing is yellow for long. Feed it from Kafka with the merchant id as the document id, as the Storage engines track's search lesson said, so redeliveries overwrite instead of duplicating; the id is also the routing key, so one merchant's updates always go to the same primary. When the support UI pages through results, use `search_after` instead of deep `from` values, because every page costs every shard. And treat yellow on the dashboard as a page-worthy event during a release window: one more node loss turns it red.
mistake: The most common mistake is choosing the shard count by habit: Elasticsearch's old default of 5 primaries, or one shard per day of logs, at whatever size that gives. It works at first, because small shards are fast. A year later the cluster has 9,000 shards of 200 MB, the cluster state is huge, every search sends hundreds of shard requests, and nodes hit `cluster.max_shards_per_node`. Or the opposite: one 400 GB shard that takes hours to recover after every reboot. People make it because the primary count must be chosen before there's any data to measure. The fix is to estimate the size first and aim for 10 to 50 GB per shard, use rollover for data that grows forever, and shrink or reindex old indices that ended up with too many tiny shards.

The cluster node names its roles, the seed hosts to find the others, and the manager-eligible nodes that vote in the first election; it binds to a real interface, so the bootstrap checks are enforced. The lab's Compose files set these as environment variables, and both turn off the security plugin, which only a laptop should do. `cluster.name` must match on every node of a cluster.

lab.title: Model a search cluster: routing, allocation, failover, health and query-then-fetch
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. No Docker needed. One test passes (the given routing hash); nine fail.

Write `shardFor`, two lines from the KDoc. A test checks it against the shards the three-node cluster chose for M-0042 to M-0054, and another splits 3 shards into 6 and checks that no document changes halves.
Write `health`, then `allocate`: replicas only, never next to a copy of their own shard, fewest copies first. Three tests check concrete placements on one, two and three nodes.

Write `nodeLeft`: unassign the node's copies and promote a replica for each lost primary, without allocating. Two tests replay the stepper: yellow, then green on two nodes after `allocate`, then red when two nodes go before any copy is rebuilt.
Write `ShardedIndex.search`: query every shard for its top `from + size`, merge, keep the page, fetch only that. The deep-page test counts the hits the shards send back. All ten pass.
hints: `shardFor`: `val slots = routingNumShards(primaries)`, then `Math.floorMod(routingHash(routing), slots) / (slots / primaries)`. Kotlin's `%` keeps the sign of a negative hash, `floorMod` doesn't.

`allocate`: for each unassigned replica, `val start = nodes.indexOf(primaryNode)`, scan `(1..nodes.size).map { nodes[(start + it) % nodes.size] }`, drop nodes that already hold a copy of the shard, then `minByOrNull { copiesOn(it).size }` keeps the first of equals.

`nodeLeft`: loop over `copiesOn(node).sortedBy { it.shard }` (a copy of the list, so you can change the copies). For a lost primary, find `copiesOf(shard).firstOrNull { !it.primary && it.node != null }`, set its `primary = true`, and set the lost copy's `primary = false`.
`search`: `compareByDescending<Hit> { it.score }.thenBy { it.id }` is the order everywhere; each shard's list is `take(from + size)`, and the page is `drop(from).take(size)` of the merged list.

drill.title: A node failure, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking: an index has 3 primaries and 1 replica on nodes A, B and C, laid out as A: p0, r2; B: p1, r0; C: p2, r1. (a) Node B dies. Write the layout and the health immediately after the manager reacts, and again a minute and a recovery later. (b) Which two nodes would have to die together to turn the index red, and why? (c) Write the routing formula, and say why the primary count can't change.

answer.src:
(a) right after: shard 1's replica on C is promoted
      A: p0, r2     C: p2, p1     unassigned: r0, r1     -> yellow
    after the 1-minute delay and peer recovery (never next to its own primary):
      A: p0, r2, r1 C: p2, p1, r0                        -> green
(b) any two whose loss takes both copies of one shard: A and C (shard 2),
    B and C (shard 1), or A and B (shard 0), before a new copy is built.
    With 3 primaries and 1 replica on 3 nodes, any two nodes do it.
(c) shard = hash(_routing) % number_of_primary_shards, _routing = _id by default
    change the divisor and most documents belong to another shard;
    reindex into a new index, or _split into a multiple of the shard count

recap: An index is a fixed number of primary shards, each a whole Lucene index; a document goes to `hash(_routing) % number_of_primary_shards` (really 768 slots for 3 shards), so the primary count is set at creation; reindex or `_split` to change it.
Replicas are full copies on other nodes, never next to their own primary; they survive node failures and serve searches, and their count can change any time. Defaults: 1 primary, 1 replica.

The cluster state (nodes, mappings, the routing table) is changed only by the elected cluster manager. Eligible nodes elect it by majority, so run three; `discovery.seed_hosts` finds peers and `cluster.initial_cluster_manager_nodes` bootstraps the first election.

A write goes to the primary (buffer plus translog), then to every in-sync replica before the ack; a refresh every second makes it searchable. A search is a scatter-gather over local indexes: one copy of every shard returns its top `from + size` ids, the coordinator merges them and fetches only the page.
A node leaves: replicas are promoted, missing copies wait 1 minute, then peer recovery rebuilds them: yellow, then green. Red means every copy of some shard is gone.
Keep shards at 10 to 50 GB; heap at half the RAM, at most about 31 GB, the rest for the page cache; `vm.max_map_count` 262,144; security on for anything but a laptop.

quiz.q: From lesson 2: the merchants index has 3 primary shards and is growing. Why does OpenSearch refuse to change `number_of_shards` to 4 in place?
options: Shard counts must be powers of two
Routing is a hash modulo the shard count, so a new count would put most documents in the wrong shard; reindex, or `_split` into 6
The cluster manager can only track 3 shards per index
Replicas would have to be deleted first
quiz.why: A document's shard is computed from its id every time it's read or written. Change the divisor and most ids map elsewhere, the way lesson 2's `hash mod S` moved 80% of the keys going from 4 nodes to 5. OpenSearch won't silently move them, so you reindex into a new index or split into a multiple (3 into 6), which works because each shard owns a range of routing slots that splits cleanly in two. Replica counts change freely.

quiz.q: A team runs two cluster-manager-eligible nodes to save money. One of them crashes. What happens?
options: The survivor becomes manager and everything continues
Searches and writes stop at once
No node can win an election, because one vote out of two isn't a majority; anything that needs the manager, such as promoting a replica or creating an index, stops
The cluster splits into two independent clusters
quiz.why: An election needs a majority of the voting nodes, and with two voters that's both of them. The survivor alone can't become manager, so nothing that changes the cluster state can happen until the other one returns. Majority voting is also what prevents the split into two clusters. With three eligible nodes, any two still form a majority.

quiz.q: Right after a data node stops, health is yellow. Which statement is true?
options: Some documents can't be found until the node returns
Every shard still has a primary, so searches return all documents, but some replicas are unassigned
Writes are refused until health is green
The cluster has lost data
quiz.why: Yellow means all primaries are assigned and at least one replica isn't. The manager promoted a replica for every primary the node held, so every document is still searchable and writable, as the Try-it's count of 13 showed. What's missing is redundancy. Red is the state where some documents can't be searched.

quiz.q: A disputes index grows from 4 primary shards to 16 (by reindexing), on the same nodes with the same data. What happens to a search by merchant name?
options: It still asks one copy of every shard, now 16 requests instead of 4, and waits for the slowest; latency usually doesn't fall and the work per search rises
Each shard holds a quarter of the documents, so the search gets about 4 times faster
It goes only to the shard that holds the merchant's documents
Nothing changes: the cluster manager answers searches from the cluster state
quiz.why: Each shard's inverted index covers only its own documents, the local index of lesson 4, so a search on anything but the routing value must ask every shard. More shards means more requests per search and more chances to hit a slow one; it adds throughput only when there are more nodes to run them. Only the `_routing` value, the id here, picks a single shard. The cluster state holds the map, not the documents.

quiz.q: A UI pages through dispute search results with `from` and `size`. On an index with 5 shards, a user asks for `from: 9990, size: 10`. How many hits do the shards send to the coordinating node?
quiz.why: No shard knows which of its hits make the global page, so each returns its own top `from + size` = 10,000 ids and scores, and the coordinator sorts 5 x 10,000 = 50,000 to keep 10. Only those 10 are fetched. That's why `index.max_result_window` stops at 10,000 by default; use `search_after` for deep paging.

flashcards.front: How does OpenSearch pick a document's shard?
flashcards.back: `hash(_routing) % number_of_primary_shards`, with `_routing` = `_id` by default and Murmur3 as the hash. A 3-shard index really uses 768 routing slots, 256 per shard.

flashcards.front: Why is the number of primary shards fixed when an index is created?
flashcards.back: Routing divides by it. A new count would put most documents in another shard. Reindex, or `_split` into a multiple.

flashcards.front: What does the elected cluster manager do?
flashcards.back: It is the only node that changes the cluster state: nodes, index metadata and the routing table. It allocates shards, promotes replicas and publishes each new version to every node.
Green: every copy assigned. Yellow: every primary assigned, some replica not. Red: some primary unassigned, so some data can't be searched.

flashcards.front: What happens in the minute after a node leaves?
flashcards.back: Its primaries' replicas are promoted at once; its other copies stay unassigned for `index.unassigned.node_left.delayed_timeout` (1m) in case it returns; then peer recovery rebuilds them.

flashcards.front: Query then fetch, in one line?
flashcards.back: Every shard returns the ids and scores of its top `from + size`; the coordinator merges them and fetches the documents of the final page only.

flashcards.front: Heap and shard size rules for OpenSearch?
flashcards.back: Heap: Xms = Xmx, half the RAM, at most about 31 GB; the rest feeds the page cache. Shards: 10 to 50 GB.

terms.plain: One of the fixed number of pieces an index is split into; a complete Lucene index that takes each write first.
A full copy of a primary shard on another node, updated on every write and used for searches and failover.
Choosing a document's shard from a hash of its routing value, its `_id` by default.
The shared map of nodes, index settings and mappings, and which shard copy lives on which node.
The elected node that changes the cluster state; `cluster_manager` nodes are eligible and vote.
Turning a shard's in-memory buffer into a new searchable segment, every second by default.
Each shard copy's write-ahead log, fsync'ed before a write is acknowledged and replayed after a crash.
Building a new shard copy by copying the primary's segments, then the operations that arrived meanwhile.

explain_back.prompt: Your team is about to run a three-node OpenSearch cluster for dispute search. Explain to a colleague how a document is stored and found across the nodes, what happens when one node dies, and the three settings decisions you'd make on day one.
explain_back.answer: The disputes index is split into a fixed number of primary shards, each a full Lucene index, and every primary has a replica on a different node. A dispute goes to the shard picked by hashing its id modulo the primary count, which is why that count is fixed when we create the index; changing it means reindexing. One node is the elected cluster manager. It keeps the map of which shard copy lives where and every node routes with that map. A write lands on the shard's primary, goes into its buffer and translog, is copied to the replica, and only then acknowledged; it becomes searchable at the next refresh, within a second. A search goes to one copy of every shard, each returns its best ids and scores, and the node we asked merges them and fetches just the page we show. If a node dies, the manager promotes the replicas of the primaries it had, health goes yellow but every dispute is still searchable, and after a minute it rebuilds the missing replicas on the other nodes and we're green again. Red would mean both copies of some shard are gone. On day one I'd choose the primary count from the expected size so shards stay between 10 and 50 GB, keep one replica and make all three nodes manager-eligible so any two can elect a manager, and give each node a 31 GB heap at most with the rest of the RAM left to the page cache, with security switched on.

deeper.body:
Document replication, where every copy indexes every document, is the default (`index.replication.type: DOCUMENT`), and it means each replica spends as much CPU as its primary. OpenSearch also offers segment replication: only the primary indexes, and replicas copy its finished segments after each refresh. Indexing throughput goes up, and replicas lag the primary by a refresh or so. OpenSearch also has search replicas, on nodes with the `search` role: copies that only serve searches, so heavy indexing and heavy searching stop competing for the same nodes.

Shard allocation awareness spreads copies across failure domains. Give each node an attribute such as `node.attr.zone: eu-west-1a` and set `cluster.routing.allocation.awareness.attributes: zone`, and the manager puts a shard's primary and replica in different zones, so losing a whole zone leaves a copy of everything. The lab's same-shard rule is the one-zone version of this.

A replica is not a backup. A bad mapping change, a script that deletes the wrong documents, or a red index after a double failure all reach every copy or none. Snapshots are the backup: `PUT _snapshot/<repo>/<name>` copies the segment files to a repository such as S3, incrementally, because segments never change once written.

Sequence numbers make recovery cheap. Every operation on a shard gets a sequence number, and every copy tracks the highest one below which it has everything (its local checkpoint). When a node comes back within the delay, its replica only needs the operations above its checkpoint, kept on the primary as a retention lease, instead of every segment again. The primary term in the Try-it's write response is the other half: after a promotion, operations from the old primary carry the old term and are rejected.

Elasticsearch shares all of this up to the 7.10 fork and has gone its own way since: in Elasticsearch 8 and 9 the defaults and some names differ (it never renamed "master"), and serverless Elasticsearch separates indexing and search tiers on object storage. The routing formula, replicas, refresh and query then fetch are the same in both.
